title: Completion and the Code for Completion by Post
subtitle: Synchronising money and the deed, executing correctly, and the solicitor's undertaking
objectives: Explain how the Law Society's Code for Completion by Post synchronises the same-day transfer of completion monies with the release of the executed TR1

State the execution formalities for a deed by an individual under section 1 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989 and by a company under section 44 of the Companies Act 2006, and identify defective execution
Explain the nature of a solicitor's undertaking given on completion and the professional consequences of breaching one

leadingAuthorities.citation: Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, s 1
leadingAuthorities.role: Sets the formalities for a valid deed executed by an individual, including signature and attestation by a witness
Sets the formalities for valid execution of a document by a company, including execution by two authorised signatories or a director and witness

leadingAuthorities.citation: Law Society Code for Completion by Post
leadingAuthorities.role: Governs the mechanics of postal (in practice, electronic) completion, synchronising release of funds and the executed transfer between solicitors acting as each other's agent

leadingAuthorities.citation: Udall v Capri Lighting Ltd [1988] QB 907
leadingAuthorities.role: Confirms that a solicitor's undertaking, once given, is a personally binding professional obligation enforceable against the solicitor regardless of the client's own conduct

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can state that completion is 'when the money moves and the deed is handed over'. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know what completion is — this lesson is about the mechanics that make it happen safely, and what happens when an undertaking is broken.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well here on recall before. Expect fact patterns testing defective execution and broken undertakings, not bare definitions.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and make sure you can state, in order, what the Code for Completion by Post actually requires the seller's solicitor to do once funds are received, before moving on.

overview.hook: On completion day, the buyer's solicitor sends several hundred thousand pounds down an electronic wire to a firm they may never have dealt with before, on the strength of nothing more than that firm's word that it will, in return, release a signed deed and hand over the keys. There is no simultaneous exchange of cash for goods across a counter. The entire system runs on a promise — the solicitor's undertaking — and on a shared code of practice that tells everyone exactly what happens, and in what order, once the money lands.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. Execution formalities under the 1989 and 2006 Acts and the Law Society's Code for Completion by Post are settled, longstanding features of conveyancing practice.

parts.heading: The problem completion by post is built to solve
parts.voice: argumentative — states the risk before presenting the solution
body: Completion in most transactions today does not involve solicitors meeting in person to exchange a deed for a banker's draft. It happens remotely: the buyer's solicitor transfers completion monies electronically, and the seller's solicitor is expected, in return and at effectively the same moment, to release the executed transfer, redeem any existing mortgage, and arrange for the keys to be released.

The obvious risk is sequencing. If funds are sent before the deed is confirmed ready, the buyer's solicitor has parted with the client's money with no simultaneous guarantee of getting anything for it. If the deed is released before funds are confirmed received, the seller is exposed the other way. Neither side can safely go first without some mechanism that makes the other side's promise reliable.

The Law Society's Code for Completion by Post exists to solve exactly this. It does so by having the seller's solicitor act, for the narrow purpose of completion, as the buyer's solicitor's agent — carrying out a defined checklist of tasks in a defined order once funds are received, on the buyer's solicitor's behalf, and confirming this by telephone.

components.definition: The Law Society's code under which the seller's solicitor acts as the buyer's solicitor's agent on completion day, carrying out an agreed sequence of steps — confirming receipt of funds, dating and releasing the transfer, redeeming existing charges — once completion monies have been received, without the two solicitors meeting in person.

interaction.prompt: Under the Code for Completion by Post, whose agent does the seller's solicitor act as for the purpose of completing the transaction?
options: The buyer's solicitor's agent
An independent agent owing no duty to either side
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The seller's solicitor takes on a defined agency role for the buyer's solicitor, which is what allows the transaction to complete without both firms meeting in person.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Reconsider the structure. The Code works precisely because the seller's solicitor agrees to act, for completion purposes, as the buyer's solicitor's agent — carrying out defined steps on the buyer's behalf.

parts.heading: What the seller's solicitor actually does once funds arrive
parts.voice: structural — sets out the sequence as a reference
body: Once the seller's solicitor confirms receipt of the completion monies specified by the buyer's solicitor, a defined sequence follows. The seller's solicitor dates the TR1 (which will already have been executed in readiness, as covered in the previous lesson), holds it to the buyer's solicitor's order, arranges for any existing mortgage on the property to be redeemed from the proceeds, and releases the keys — typically by telephoning the estate agent to confirm the buyer can collect them.

The seller's solicitor then telephones the buyer's solicitor to confirm completion has taken place. From that moment, the buyer becomes entitled to possession, even though registration of the transfer at the Land Registry will follow afterwards — registration is what perfects legal title, but the transaction has completed in the practical sense once this sequence is done.

The Code's discipline is what makes this safe: the buyer's solicitor is trusting that a firm they may never meet will carry out a fixed checklist correctly and promptly, purely because that firm has agreed to be bound by the Code and has given the completion undertakings that go with it.

components.title: Sequence under the Code for Completion by Post
components.description: The order of events once the buyer's solicitor sends completion monies.

nodes.label: Buyer's solicitor sends completion monies electronically
Seller's solicitor confirms receipt of the funds specified
Seller's solicitor dates the already-executed TR1 and holds it to the buyer's solicitor's order
Seller's solicitor arranges redemption of any existing mortgage from the proceeds
Seller's solicitor releases the keys, typically via the estate agent
Seller's solicitor telephones the buyer's solicitor to confirm completion

components.textAlternative: The buyer's solicitor sends completion monies electronically. The seller's solicitor confirms receipt, dates the already-executed TR1 and holds it to the buyer's solicitor's order, arranges redemption of any existing mortgage, releases the keys (typically via the estate agent), and telephones the buyer's solicitor to confirm completion has taken place.

interaction.prompt: Put these steps of a postal completion in the correct order.
items: Seller's solicitor confirms receipt of the funds
Seller's solicitor dates the TR1 and arranges mortgage redemption
Seller's solicitor releases the keys and confirms completion by phone
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the Code's sequence — confirmation of funds always comes before the deed is dated and released, never the other way round.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — the seller's solicitor must confirm receipt of funds before doing anything with the deed, keys or mortgage redemption, not simultaneously or in advance.

parts.heading: Executing a deed correctly: individuals
parts.voice: reference-style — sets out the formality precisely
body: The TR1 must be executed as a deed, and the formalities for an individual are set out in section 1 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989. The document must make clear on its face that it is intended to be a deed, it must be validly executed as a deed, and it must be delivered.

Valid execution by an individual means the document is signed by that person in the presence of a witness who attests the signature — that is, the witness also signs, confirming they saw the individual sign. A document signed by the individual alone, with no witness present at the moment of signature, is not validly executed as a deed, however clearly it is labelled as one.

This matters in practice because a defectively executed TR1 does not transfer legal title, however much both sides believe completion has happened. SQE1 fact patterns often hide the defect in a small detail — a witness who signs later, from memory, rather than at the moment of signature — and expect you to spot that this fails the formality.

components.citation: Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, s 1
components.text: An instrument shall not be a deed unless it makes clear on its face that it is intended to be a deed and it is validly executed as a deed by the person making it or, as the case may be, one or more of the parties to it. An instrument is validly executed as a deed by an individual if, and only if, it is signed by him in the presence of a witness who attests the signature, or at his direction and in his presence and the presence of two witnesses who each attest the signature.
elements: The document must make clear on its face it is intended to be a deed
It must be signed by the individual (or at their direction, in their presence)
A witness must be present at the moment of signature and must attest (sign to confirm they witnessed it)

interaction.prompt: An individual seller signs the TR1 alone at home, with no one else present, and posts it to their solicitor. A colleague at the firm, who did not see the seller sign, later adds their own signature as 'witness' on the same page. Has the TR1 been validly executed as a deed?
options: Yes — the document has both a signature and a witness signature, which is all that is required
No — the witness must be present at the moment of signature and attest it there and then; signing later without having witnessed it does not satisfy section 1
Yes, provided the colleague is a qualified solicitor
No, because only a notary can witness a deed
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A witness who was not actually present when the individual signed cannot validly attest the signature, whatever their qualification — the deed is defectively executed.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Focus on what 'attest' requires: the witness must actually observe the signature at the time. A signature added afterwards by someone who was not present does not satisfy section 1, regardless of who that person is.

parts.heading: Executing a deed correctly: companies
parts.voice: structural — sets out the company-specific route as a contrast
body: Where a party to the transfer is a company, execution is governed by section 44 of the Companies Act 2006, which offers two valid routes: execution by two authorised signatories (for example two directors, or a director and the company secretary), or execution by a single director whose signature is witnessed and attested.

Unlike the individual route, a company can validly execute a deed with only one director's signature — provided that signature is witnessed, exactly as an individual's would need to be. What a company cannot do is execute validly with only one director's signature and no witness at all; that satisfies neither route under section 44.

SQE1 questions on this topic often test whether you can spot the difference between the two valid company routes and a defective attempt that falls between them — for instance, a single director signing alone with no witness, mistakenly believing that a company seal or letterhead is enough to cure the defect.

components.label: Companies Act 2006, s 44: valid routes to execution
points: Route 1: signature by two authorised signatories (for example two directors, or a director and the secretary)
Route 2: signature by a single director, with that signature witnessed and attested
Invalid: a single director's signature with no witness satisfies neither route

interaction.prompt: A company's TR1 is signed by a single director only, with no witness present, but the company's common seal is also affixed. Is this validly executed under section 44 of the Companies Act 2006?
options: Yes — affixing the company seal always cures any defect in signature
No — a single director's signature must be witnessed to satisfy section 44; the seal does not substitute for that requirement
Yes, provided the director is also the company secretary
No, because a company can never execute a deed with only one signature
interaction.trapExplanation: It is tempting to assume a company seal is a universal fix, but section 44 does not treat sealing as an alternative to its two defined signature routes — a single unwitnessed director's signature remains defective regardless of a seal.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The seal is not one of the two routes section 44 provides; a single director's signature must be witnessed, or a second authorised signatory must also sign.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Re-check the two valid routes under section 44 — neither involves the company seal curing an unwitnessed single-director signature.

parts.heading: The undertaking: a promise a solicitor cannot walk back from
parts.voice: case-narrative — grounds the doctrine in what breach actually costs
body: Everything in this lesson — sending money before physically holding the deed, releasing a deed before physically holding the money — depends on solicitors trusting each other's word. That trust is formalised through the undertaking: a statement, given by a solicitor in a professional capacity, that they will do (or refrain from doing) something, or confirming that a specified thing has been done or will happen.

An undertaking is not simply advisory. Once given, it is a personally binding professional obligation on the solicitor who gives it, enforceable by the profession's regulator and, in appropriate cases, by the court — and, critically, it binds the solicitor personally, regardless of what their client subsequently does or fails to do. If a seller's solicitor undertakes to redeem an existing mortgage from the completion proceeds and the client later instructs them not to, or the funds turn out to be insufficient, the solicitor remains personally on the hook to honour the undertaking or answer for the consequences.

This is why undertakings are treated with real weight in practice: a solicitor who gives one carelessly, or breaches one, faces professional consequences that can include disciplinary action and personal liability, independent of anything their client does. It is also precisely why the Code for Completion by Post can work at all — the buyer's solicitor is willing to send money to a stranger firm because that firm's undertaking to comply with the Code is worth relying on.

components.factsShort: A solicitor gave an undertaking in the course of acting for a client; a dispute arose over whether the undertaking could be enforced against the solicitor personally.
components.ratioShort: A solicitor's undertaking given in a professional capacity is a personally binding obligation, enforceable against the solicitor regardless of the client's own instructions or conduct.

expanded.facts: The case concerned the enforceability of an undertaking given by a solicitor in the course of professional dealings, where the solicitor argued the undertaking should not bind them personally in the circumstances that had unfolded.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal confirmed the well-established principle that a solicitor who gives an undertaking in a professional capacity is personally bound by it, and the court retains a supervisory jurisdiction to enforce undertakings given by solicitors as officers of the court.
expanded.significance: The case is cited for the proposition, central to conveyancing practice, that a solicitor cannot avoid personal responsibility for an undertaking by pointing to a client's later conduct or instructions — the undertaking is the solicitor's own binding promise.

interaction.prompt: Two scenarios. In which has the solicitor most clearly breached a personally binding undertaking?
interaction.scenarioA: A solicitor undertakes to redeem the seller's mortgage from completion proceeds, then fails to do so because the client withdrew instructions to release the funds for that purpose.
interaction.scenarioB: A solicitor tells the other side, informally and without giving a formal undertaking, that they 'expect' the transaction to complete by Friday, and it completes the following Monday instead.
interaction.explanation: In A, a formal undertaking was given and not honoured — the client's later instructions do not excuse the solicitor, who remains personally bound. In B, no undertaking was given at all; an informal expression of expectation, without more, does not create the same binding professional obligation.

testPool.prompt: Under the Law Society's Code for Completion by Post, whose agent does the seller's solicitor act as when completing the transaction?
options: The buyer's solicitor's agent
The Land Registry's agent
The mortgage lender's agent only
No agency relationship is created
testPool.explanation: The Code has the seller's solicitor act as the buyer's solicitor's agent for the limited purpose of carrying out the defined completion steps once funds are received.

testPool.prompt: Which document is dated and released to the buyer's solicitor's order once the seller's solicitor confirms receipt of completion monies?
options: The requisitions on title
The already-executed TR1
The original signed contract from exchange
The redemption statement
testPool.explanation: The TR1, executed in advance of completion day, is dated by the seller's solicitor and held to the buyer's solicitor's order once funds are confirmed received.

testPool.prompt: Under section 1 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, what must happen for an individual's signature on a deed to be validly attested?
options: A witness must sign at any point after the document is fully completed
A witness must be present at the moment of signature and sign to confirm they witnessed it
The document must be notarised by an independent notary
The signature must be given in the presence of two witnesses in every case
testPool.explanation: Attestation requires the witness to be present when the individual signs and to sign themselves to confirm they witnessed it — signing later, without having been present, does not satisfy the requirement.

testPool.prompt: Under section 44 of the Companies Act 2006, which of the following is a valid route to execution of a deed by a company?
options: Signature by a single director, with that signature witnessed and attested
Signature by any employee of the company, witnessed or not
Affixing the company letterhead alone
Signature by the company's accountant
testPool.explanation: Section 44 provides two valid routes: two authorised signatories, or a single director whose signature is witnessed. A single director's unwitnessed signature, or signature by an unauthorised employee, satisfies neither route.

testPool.prompt: A trainee believes completion is only 'really' finished once the transfer is registered at the Land Registry, and that nothing before then counts as completion. Is this an accurate way to describe the transaction's status?
options: Yes — nothing about completion has legal effect until registration occurs

No — completion occurs when the Code for Completion by Post sequence is carried out (funds received, deed released, keys handed over); registration afterwards perfects legal title but is a separate step
Yes, because the buyer has no rights at all until the register is updated
No, because registration happens automatically the moment contracts are exchanged
testPool.trapExplanation: It is easy to collapse 'completion' and 'registration' into one event because both feel like the finishing line, but they are legally distinct steps — completion is a practical and contractual event; registration is what perfects legal title afterwards.
testPool.explanation: Completion (money and deed changing hands under the Code) and registration (which perfects legal title at the Land Registry) are sequential but separate steps, and conflating them misdescribes what has actually happened on completion day.

testPool.prompt: A company's TR1 is signed by two people: one director, and one person who is not a director, company secretary or otherwise an authorised signatory, but who happened to be in the office at the time. Is this validly executed under section 44 of the Companies Act 2006?
options: Yes — any two people signing on the company's behalf satisfies section 44
No — two authorised signatories (such as two directors, or a director and the secretary) are required for that route, and an unauthorised person's signature does not satisfy it
Yes, provided the two signatures are witnessed by a third person
No, because a company can never execute with fewer than three signatures
testPool.trapExplanation: It is tempting to think 'two signatures' automatically satisfies section 44 because the two-signatory route is often summarised loosely — but the route specifically requires two authorised signatories, not simply two people who happened to sign.
testPool.explanation: The two-signatory route under section 44 requires the signatories to be authorised (such as two directors, or a director and the secretary); an unauthorised bystander's signature does not complete that route.

testPool.prompt: A seller's solicitor gives an undertaking to redeem the seller's mortgage from completion proceeds. After completion, the client instructs the solicitor to use the proceeds for something else instead, and the mortgage is not redeemed. Can the solicitor rely on the client's instructions as a defence to breach of undertaking?
options: Yes — solicitors are only ever agents and must follow client instructions above all else
No — an undertaking is a personally binding professional obligation on the solicitor, which the client's later instructions do not excuse
Yes, provided the solicitor informs the other side promptly after the event
No, but only if the undertaking was given in writing rather than orally
testPool.trapExplanation: It feels natural to think client instructions always override a solicitor's other obligations, but an undertaking is precisely the kind of professional obligation that binds the solicitor personally — client conduct afterwards does not excuse a breach.
testPool.explanation: Udall v Capri Lighting Ltd confirms that an undertaking given in a professional capacity binds the solicitor personally; a client's later instructions, however clearly given, do not provide a defence to breach.

testPool.prompt: A buyer's solicitor is due to send completion monies under the Code for Completion by Post. In what order should the key events happen?
options: Funds are sent and confirmed received before the seller's solicitor dates and releases the TR1
The TR1 is released before any funds are sent, on trust that payment will follow
Funds and the TR1 are exchanged simultaneously in person at a meeting
The keys are released before completion monies are even calculated
testPool.explanation: The Code's sequencing exists precisely to avoid either side going first without protection: funds are sent and receipt confirmed before the seller's solicitor takes the steps that release the deed and keys.

testPool.prompt: An individual seller's TR1 is signed by the seller alone, at home, with a neighbour present who then also signs as a witness immediately afterwards, having watched the seller sign. Has this satisfied section 1 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989?
options: No — only a solicitor or notary can act as a witness to a deed
Yes — the witness was present at the moment of signature and attested it, which is what section 1 requires of an individual
No — two witnesses are always required for an individual's signature
Yes, but only if the neighbour is also a party to the transaction
testPool.explanation: Section 1 requires a witness present at the moment of signature who then attests it — there is no requirement that the witness be a solicitor, notary or other qualified professional, and one witness suffices for an individual signing personally.

testPool.prompt: A company executing a TR1 has it signed by its sole director only, with no witness present and no second signatory. What is the status of the execution under section 44 of the Companies Act 2006?
options: Valid — a sole director can always execute alone
Invalid — this satisfies neither the two-authorised-signatory route nor the single-director-with-witness route
Valid, provided the company has only one director in total
Invalid, but only if the company is a public company
testPool.explanation: A single director's signature with no witness and no second authorised signatory falls between the two valid routes under section 44 and is therefore not a valid execution.

testPool.prompt: A buyer's solicitor is reluctant to send completion monies to an unfamiliar firm acting for the seller. What feature of the transaction is specifically designed to make that reliance reasonable?
options: The seller's estate agent's personal guarantee
The seller's solicitor's undertaking to comply with the Code for Completion by Post, which is personally binding on that solicitor
The buyer's own solicitor's professional indemnity insurance
An informal assurance given by the seller's solicitor over email with no undertaking wording
testPool.explanation: The system depends on the seller's solicitor's undertaking to follow the Code being a personally binding professional obligation — that is what makes it reasonable for the buyer's solicitor to send funds to an unfamiliar firm in the first place.

testPool.prompt: According to section 1 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, which of the following is required for a document to be a valid deed executed by an individual?
options: The document must make clear on its face that it is intended to be a deed, and be validly executed and delivered
The document must be registered at the Land Registry before it can take effect as a deed
The document must be executed in the presence of a solicitor specifically
The document must be sealed with a wax seal
testPool.explanation: Section 1 requires the document to make clear it is intended as a deed, be validly executed (signed and, for an individual, witnessed), and delivered — there is no requirement for a wax seal or for execution specifically before a solicitor.

testPool.prompt: A document is clearly labelled 'This is a Deed' and is signed by the individual seller, but there is no witness present at all. Applying section 1 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, is this validly executed?
options: Yes — labelling the document as a deed is sufficient on its own
No — valid execution by an individual requires signature in the presence of an attesting witness, which is missing here
Yes, provided the document is also delivered to the other party
No, because individuals can never execute deeds without two witnesses
testPool.explanation: Labelling a document as a deed satisfies only one of the section 1 requirements; without an attesting witness present at signature, execution by an individual is not valid, however the document is described.

testPool.prompt: A company's TR1 is executed by two directors, each signing in the presence of the other but with no independent witness to either signature. Applying section 44 of the Companies Act 2006, is this validly executed?
options: No — both directors' signatures must additionally be independently witnessed
Yes — signature by two authorised signatories (such as two directors) is itself a valid route under section 44, with no witness required for that route
No — a company can never execute with only two signatures
Yes, but only if the company also affixes its common seal
testPool.explanation: The two-authorised-signatory route under section 44 does not require an independent witness — witnessing is only required under the alternative single-director route. Two directors signing together validly executes the deed without a witness.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring trap in this lesson is treating completion, execution formalities and undertakings as separate bureaucratic hurdles rather than one connected system: the Code for Completion by Post only works because execution has already happened correctly, and because the undertaking behind it is genuinely, personally binding on the solicitor who gives it.
